title.text: Saint Raymond of Peñafort Parish Church (Malaueg Church)

title_en.text: Saint Raymond of Peñafort Parish Church (Malaueg Church)

tagline.text: A 17th-century brick fortress church in the Cordillera foothills

location.label: Location
location.text: Poblacion, Rizal (formerly Malaueg), Cagayan, beside the municipal hall

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: November–May dry season (check road conditions in the rainy season)

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: 1–2 hours at the church (a day trip from Tuguegarao)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱800–2,500 (per person, round trip by van, jeepney and tricycle from Tuguegarao, lodging excluded)

children.text: Malaueg Church is the parish church of Saint Raymond of Peñafort in the center of Rizal, Cagayan, a brick church founded by the Dominicans in the early 1600s. It was declared a National Cultural Treasure in 2001, and because it is far from Tuguegarao, it remains a quiet heritage site that few travelers visit.

Rizal is a mountain town at the western edge of Cagayan, in the eastern foothills of the Cordillera. It borders Apayao, so geographically it feels closer to the Cordillera, while administratively it belongs to Cagayan. The town's old name was Malaueg, and the church is still called by several names: Malaueg Church, Rizal Church, and the Parish Church of Saint Raymond of Peñafort. The name is said to be related to an Ibanag word meaning creek or river. It is an active parish under the Archdiocese of Tuguegarao, located in the Poblacion right next to the municipal hall.

Its history begins with the Dominican missions. English Wikipedia says the Dominican priests officially established Malaueg in 1607 and that the foundations of the present church were laid on November 26, 1617. A travel blog adds that in 1607 a first church dedicated to Saint Raymond was built through the efforts of the local chieftain Luis Pagulayan, and that in 1608 the Dominicans accepted the place as a mission and used it as a base for reaching the Cordillera and bringing down people who had retreated to the mountains. During the rebellion of Caguenga and Furuganan from 1608 to 1610, the convent was burned, and Fr. Francisco Mola built a new church in 1617, which was in turn damaged by a fire in 1641. The present building is said to have been blessed again in 1651. The Wikipedia entry for the town gives even earlier years such as 1590 and 1597, so sources differ slightly on dates. If an exact date matters, please check the wording of the National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP) marker on the facade yourself.

In architecture, this church differs from the other Dominican churches of the Cagayan Valley. Wikipedia describes it as built mostly of fired brick, smaller in size and more novel in design, with loosely laid brickwork that gives it an earthy texture. Travel pieces such as Wikivoyage and Langyaw, on the other hand, describe it as stonework piled from river stones of the Matalag River. Since the descriptions of the material differ, it is fun to look closely at the walls on site. The facade has a rounded arched doorway, and a plastered white wall finished with a small triangular pediment. Niches for statues of saints flank the door, rectangular windows in triangular frames sit above, and a cross relief is carved on the topmost pediment. On the left of the facade stands a three-level bell tower with a conical roof and pointed finials at the corners of each level.

Its character as a fortress church also makes the place special. Wikivoyage notes that the church also served as a fortress against raids by the Kalinga and Isneg people of Apayao. When you recall that the mission post sat at the gateway where people came down from the Cordillera, the thick walls and small size make sense. The church and its convent are also considered the most intact church complex of the 17th century in the Cagayan Valley, and together with the churches of Lal-lo and San Pablo they are counted among the few surviving 17th-century monuments showing the region's early building boom. The National Museum declared the church a National Cultural Treasure in 2001. Whether it is worth a trip for its own sake depends on your taste. It is not a flashy tourist attraction. The town is quiet, and an older travel account even mentions that there was no market or eatery in town. What you get instead is the journey up from Tuguegarao, the texture of river stones and bricks, and the stillness of a churchyard with few visitors. It suits people who tour Spanish-era churches like a pilgrimage, those interested in the Dominican heritage of the Cagayan Valley, and those who want to see a little-known National Cultural Treasure in person. The church itself takes only an hour or two to see, so it is more efficient to combine it with other sights in the area.

This church was declared a National Cultural Treasure by the National Museum in 2001. It is treated as cultural property that shows the traces of Spanish-era missions rather than just a single building, so rather than only taking photos, we recommend looking slowly at the outer walls and the bell tower.

blocks.title: Humble walls of brick and river stone

children.text: The earthy outer walls, where fired brick and river stone come together, stand out most. Because sources describe the material differently, step close and compare the way the wall is laid yourself. You will probably notice first how small the church is and how thick its walls are.

blocks.title: A three-level bell tower with a conical roof

children.text: The three-level bell tower on the left of the facade is known for its conical roof and corner finials. It stays in view from anywhere in the churchyard, so walk around once to find a good spot for photos.

blocks.title: A facade of triangular pediment and arched door

children.text: The facade, made of an arched main door, a white plastered wall, a small triangular pediment, saint niches on both sides of the door and a cross relief at the top, is restrained in decoration. It is fun to compare with other churches in the region.
On the facade is a marker set up by the National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP) with a short history. Where sources disagree on dates, check the marker on site.

blocks.title: A mission base that served as a fortress

children.text: It is explained that the church served as a fortress against raids coming down from the Cordillera. Picture the town's location together with the thick walls of the church, and you can see how remote the Dominican missions of that time were.

blocks.title: Everyday life of a working parish

children.text: This is a parish where believers still attend Mass, not a tourist facility. Please keep quiet during Mass and prayer, and we recommend modest clothing when you go inside. Check Mass times with the local parish.

blocks.title: The town's story and surrounding nature

children.text: Rizal is a town formed from the old Malaueg and Mauanan, and nearby natural sights such as Mount Annaguan, the ecopark in Mauanan and the Blue Lagoon in Masi are mentioned. If you plan to add them to your church visit, check whether they are currently open.

items.title: Day trip from Tuguegarao
items.subtitle: Go up early, see the church, and come back down

children.text: Confirm where the vans or jeepneys to Rizal board in Tuguegarao. Vehicles commonly wait until they fill up, so it is best to set out early.
Arrive in town and look first at the church facade and the NHCP marker. Also notice the cross relief on the pediment above the door and the niches on both sides of it.
Walk around the church to look at the three-level bell tower and the way bricks and river stones are laid in the outer walls, and if there is no Mass, go inside and look around quietly.
Have a simple meal in town and look for local snacks such as sinabalu, rice cake roasted in a bamboo tube. Check where it is sold locally.
Confirm the return transport and set off for Tuguegarao. There are records that return vehicles are few, so move early in the afternoon.

An older travel account says the return vehicle ran only the next morning. That may have changed, so ask locally about the last departure before you leave, and if in doubt use a private or chartered vehicle.

items.title: Two-day overnight plan
items.subtitle: Stay a night in Rizal and see the surroundings

children.text: Travel from Tuguegarao to Rizal and look around the church and the town.
Drop your bags at a lodging in town (Wikivoyage lists the Casa Carolina pension house in Poblacion) and ask locally about nearby natural sights.
Walk around the church once more, quietly take in the atmosphere of the morning Mass, and return to Tuguegarao.
Information on lodging and surrounding sights is scarce, so ask the municipal hall or the parish before you leave.
Philippine Airlines and Cebu Pacific are known to fly from Manila to Tuguegarao Airport (TUG) daily, and the flight takes about
1 hour 10 minutes
. Check schedules and fares with the airlines.
From Tuguegarao to Rizal you travel by land.
Victory Liner from the Kamias terminal in Quezon City is said to take about
12 hours
to Tuguegarao. Overnight travel is typical, so plan for your stamina and schedule.
After getting off in Tuguegarao, transfer to a vehicle bound for Rizal.
Wikivoyage says passenger vans and jeepneys run from Tuguegarao to Rizal, and that you may wait an indefinite time for the vehicle to fill. A travel blog says a jeepney ride takes about
2 hours
. By private car it is also said to take about
2 hours
, and the road distance is estimated at about
125km
The usual route goes north from Tuguegarao via Tuao. In the rainy season the Itawes Bridge can be submerged, forcing a long detour toward Kalinga, so check road conditions before you leave.
An older travel account mentions dirt road, makeshift bridges and a river ferry on the approach. Things may have changed, so check the latest information.
Tricycles are the main transport in town. The church is next to the municipal hall, so it can be reached on foot from the town center.
Outlying barangays have rough roads, and a 4WD is said to be needed.
Rizal's average daily high is about
and its average low about
, with annual rainfall of about 1,695 mm and around 220 rainy days a year. November to May, when there is less rain, is more comfortable for travel and walking.

In the rainy season from June to November, roads and rivers can get worse, so check local conditions before departure. There is guidance that political tension can arise during election season (the first half of every third year), so follow the latest news.

items.note: It is a parish church, and no separate fee information was found

Rizal does not have many places to stay. Wikivoyage lists the Casa Carolina pension house in Poblacion as the only lodging in town, but this may change, so confirm before booking. The easiest approach is to stay in the larger city of Tuguegarao and make a day trip.

Local foods mentioned for the town include sinabalu, a rice cake roasted in a bamboo tube, and kasasut, smoked pork jerky. Kasasut is said to be eaten for breakfast. Shops may open and close depending on the season, so ask locally.
Before you leave, contact the parish (the number listed on Wikivoyage is +63 967 990 1490) or the municipal hall to confirm Mass times and whether the church is open. The number may change.
Vehicles from Tuguegarao to Rizal may wait until they fill, so go to the boarding point early in the morning.
Return vehicles may be few, so leave early in the afternoon. A private or chartered vehicle makes your schedule much freer.
There is guidance that the Itawes Bridge can be submerged in the rainy season, so check road conditions first.
Refrain from taking photos and making loud noise during Mass or prayer, and we recommend modest clothing inside the church.
The walls and bell tower are old cultural property, so do not rub them with your hands or climb on them.
Restaurants and markets may be few, so bring plenty of water and snacks.
Many places need cash and ATMs may be rare, so exchange money and withdraw cash in Tuguegarao beforehand.

Rizal is a mountain town and access roads may be in poor condition. There is guidance that bridges can be submerged in the rainy season and that political tension can arise in election season, so check the latest news before you leave.
We could not confirm visiting hours, admission, or Mass times. Please ask the parish.
Return public transport may stop running, so decide on lodging or transport in advance.
Shops and facilities in town may be few.
Outlying barangays have rough roads, and a 4WD is said to be needed.
Political tension and safety advisories change often, so check the Korean Ministry of Foreign Affairs overseas travel advisories and local government notices.
The provincial capital of Cagayan, about
2 hours
from Rizal by land. It is the gateway reached by air and bus, and the center for accommodation.
A limestone cave in Peñablanca near Tuguegarao that fits well into a Cagayan itinerary. It lies in a different direction from Rizal, so plan it separately.
A mountain on the Poblacion side of town, described as offering views of the town and toward Apayao and Kalinga from the summit. Check locally whether it is open and how to get there.

blocks.title: Mauanan Ecopark and Masi Blue Lagoon

children.text: An ecopark in Mauanan and a freshwater natural pool in Masi are mentioned, but the roads are rough and their opening status may change, so check locally.
